This app is used to scan and connect Bluetooth devices.

Features:
- Scan nearby Bluetooth devices
- Display saved Bluetooth devices
- Support Bluetooth device connection

Please click the button above to request Bluetooth permission to use the app features.
Click Start Scanning button to search for devices

Release the buttons to move the pointer
Short press for left click, long press for right click
The connected device may not support the numeric keypad. Template input that relies on it (Alt + digits) may not work.
The app cannot read the keyboard layout of the connected device, so pick the one that matches it. If the two differ, the keys will type the wrong characters.

When sending a template, note that templates use US key positions: if the host layout is not US (French AZERTY, German QWERTZ, Russian, Arabic and so on), switch the host to a US keyboard first; for Korean, Japanese and the like the letter keys are replaced but match US in English mode, so switching to English (alphanumeric) mode is enough.
Turning a charset off only removes it from the template editor’s list; templates that already use it keep working.

What this template does, and any host setup it needs
No templates yet. Tap “New” to create one.

How to use: set the charset for your environment (the default charset follows the UI language; switch it to Unicode for Word) -> turn the numpad on -> switch to the IME of your language (Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean: switch to the US keyboard) -> type the text in the text box and send it

Notes:

1. The default charset follows the UI language and is the OEM code page of that language on the host (Simplified Chinese GBK, Traditional Chinese Big5, Japanese windows-31j, Korean windows-949, English: IBM437 in the US, IBM850 in the UK/international (the US page is used when the region is unknown), Western European languages IBM850, Russian IBM866, Arabic IBM720, Hindi US-ASCII), which is the page to use in other Windows apps; switch it to Unicode for Word. Alt Code types the code on the numpad, so turn the numpad on first (Num Lock).

2. The language-to-OEM-code-page table can be looked up behind the circled question mark next to the charset. Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese and Korean use one and the same code page for ANSI and OEM, so just pick the OEM template. Alt Code does not work when the host OEMCP is 65001 (UTF-8).

3. Without a leading zero this is the OEM variant of the Windows native Alt Code mechanism (with a leading zero it is the ANSI variant).

4. With the Microsoft IME of Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese or Korean, switch to the US keyboard (or the older-compatible IME mode / a third-party IME): those IMEs fix OEM input to IBM437 and ANSI input to windows-1252, and Word outputs 2 characters.

How to use: set the charset for your environment (the default charset follows the UI language; switch it to Unicode for Word) -> turn the numpad on -> switch to the IME of your language (Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean: the OEM version is recommended) -> type the text in the text box and send it

Notes:

1. The default charset follows the UI language and is the ANSI code page of that language on the host (Simplified Chinese GBK, Traditional Chinese Big5, Japanese windows-31j, Korean windows-949, English and Western European languages windows-1252, Russian windows-1251, Arabic windows-1256, Hindi US-ASCII), which is the page to use in other Windows apps; switch it to Unicode for Word. Alt Code types the code on the numpad, so turn the numpad on first (Num Lock).

2. The language-to-ANSI-code-page table can be looked up behind the circled question mark next to the charset. Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese and Korean use one and the same code page for ANSI and OEM, so just pick the OEM template. Alt Code does not work when the host ACP is 65001 (UTF-8).

3. With a leading zero this is the ANSI variant of Windows native Alt Code (without a leading zero it is the OEM variant).

4. With Rime for Traditional Chinese a leading zero means Big5 and no leading zero means GBK.

How to use: open the input point of a program that supports RichEdit -> adjust the IME (Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean: use English mode) -> type the text in the text box and send it (the template types u+ and the hex code, then presses Alt+X)

Notes:

Alt+X is the inline conversion built into RichEdit (Word’s text engine). No need to check the code page or change the charset, and the numpad is not used.

With the caret right after a hex code, pressing it turns the code into the character in place; but since the code is variable length, to convert exactly that piece you must select it or type u+ first (that is what the u+ in this template is for, and the prefix is deleted together with the conversion).

Works only in RichEdit hosts, searchable by app name:
Supported: every Word version, the Outlook mail body, OneNote, Windows 11 Notepad, WordPad (removed in Windows 11 24H2), the commit dialogs of TortoiseSVN / Git;
Others: not in Excel, browsers, VS Code or plain PowerPoint text boxes (PPT only in the equation editor). French Word uses Alt+C.

How to use: switch the current input source to Unicode Hex Input (System Settings -> Keyboard -> Input Sources) -> type the text in the text box and send it (the template holds Option, types 4 hex digits, then releases Option so the character lands)

Notes:

1. The code must be zero padded to 4 digits: this input source takes exactly 4 hex digits per call, so the code placeholder in the template carries pad=4 - anything shorter gets leading zeros, for example 中 is 4E2D and A must be written 0041; without the padding those digits stand for a different code point.

2. The charset is UTF-16 and should not be changed: supplementary characters (emoji etc.) are split into two Option+xxxx calls, one per UTF-16 code unit, and macOS merges the two surrogates into one character itself - 😀 is D83D and DE00, two calls. Switching to Unicode would send 5 hex digits, which this input source does not take.

3. It needs the input source to be Unicode Hex Input first - under a normal keyboard layout Option just types symbols. Switching it is up to the user (the template does not do it); switch back afterwards, or the Option+digit shortcuts of your daily typing will be taken over.

4. This preset is not verified on a real machine: there was no macOS device at hand, so the timing may vary between system versions. If it does nothing, first try Option+4E2D by hand on the host and compare with the template timing (that is what the unverified in the name is about).

How to use: no host setup needed - type the text in the text box and send it (the template presses Ctrl+Shift+U and releases it, types the hex code digits, then confirms with Space)

Notes:

1. This sequence can be pressed in two ways and this template uses the discrete one: press Ctrl+Shift+U and release it at once (the system then shows an underlined u), type the hex digits, and press Space to commit. The other way is to hold Ctrl+Shift down, type u and the digits, then let go to commit by itself - the commit then depends on the host, so the device cannot tell when it happened, and this template does not use it.

2. The charset is Unicode and does not need to be changed: write 1 to 6 hex digits, no zero padding, and no UTF-16 surrogate pair split as on macOS - supplementary characters (emoji etc.) go in with one call.

3. The host needs a desktop input-method framework (GTK / IBus / Fcitx); desktop Linux and ChromeOS ship one, so it works out of the box. A few programs grab this shortcut for themselves, and it will not work in them.

4. Space is the commit key; Enter works as well - to switch, change the last step to tap Enter.

5. Leave the input method a moment after the shortcut to settle its internal state, or the first few hex digits land in the text box as plain letters. The 50 ms key gap in the template header is that buffer; do not shorten it.

The host keyboard is not a US layout, so the keys will type other characters: switch the host to a US keyboard (Windows) or add a US keyboard input method (Linux) before sending; the Unicode Hex Input on macOS is US based already.
The letter keys of the host keyboard are not Latin letters (Korean, Japanese and the like): switch to English (alphanumeric) mode before sending - in that mode the 26 letter keys match a US keyboard.
Character %1$d “%2$s” (U+%3$s) cannot be encoded with charset %4$s; sending it would drop that character. Check the charset or the help next to it, or check whether the text is wrong.
The sample has a character that cannot be encoded: “%1$s” (U+%2$s) is not encodable with %3$s and is skipped when expanding.
These templates contain errors. Open them in the editor to fix:
Template cannot type text yet — fix it before sending
No steps yet. Use “Add step” to create one.
On the right is the charset each language uses on Windows. Write the canonical name (the bold monospaced one) in the template; the aliases below it are accepted as well.

Note: most charsets do not contain all of Unicode, so characters they lack cannot be sent (you are told before sending); and some charsets use different code points for the same character (windows-1252 vs IBM850, GBK vs Big5), so picking the wrong page types other characters. Use Unicode or UTF-16 to cover everything.
Use this one in Word (Alt Code is overridden)
English (UK / international) · Spanish · French · Portuguese · German (oem)
All modern languages (unicode) · full code points (UTF-32 without zero padding, 1-6 digits)
Supplementary-plane characters are sent as 2 units (UTF-16 code units)
Modifiers: the next add wraps into a chord
Keys: one tap adds one “tap” step
Hold and gap for each digit come from the template\'s hold / gap parameters.
The whole group is pressed and released together; “Split” gives the equivalent separate steps.
Split turns “tap” into “down” + “up”, so the key stays pressed until the matching release step.
Modifier key: it is pressed/released by this step.
This line was not recognized. Rewrite it as one valid step, e.g. “down Alt”, “sleep 20” or “<code>”.

<code> is disabled: the template cannot be used to type text
